GEO-RIGHT-01.remember: Pythagoras. If altitude h splits hypotenuse c into p,q: h²=pq, a²=cp, b²=cq, ab=ch. Hypotenuse twice a leg -> 30° opposite that leg.
GEO-RIGHT-01.link: Right-triangle structure is often shorter than Stewart, coordinates, or trig.
GEO-RIGHT-01.why: The altitude to the hypotenuse creates two smaller triangles similar to the original, generating the projection identities.
GEO-RIGHT-01.notice: Diameter, explicit 90°, altitude to hypotenuse, or hypotenuse = 2×leg.
GEO-RIGHT-01.try: Mark every right angle and ask whether similarity or a special triangle closes the problem.
GEO-RIGHT-01.contrast: Do not use a general formula before exploiting the special right-triangle theorem already present.
GEO-RIGHT-01.example: If h=6 is the altitude to the hypotenuse, c≥12 because h²=pq≤((p+q)/2)²=(c/2)².

GEO-MEDIAN-01.remember: Centroid G divides each median 2:1 from the vertex. Apollonius: m_a²=(2b²+2c²-a²)/4.
GEO-MEDIAN-01.link: Classify a vertex-to-side segment before choosing Stewart. Median -> Apollonius first.
GEO-MEDIAN-01.why: The midpoint condition fixes the split of the opposite side, allowing a strong squared-length identity and a simple centroid vector relation.
GEO-MEDIAN-01.notice: Midpoint on the opposite side, “median”, centroid, perpendicular medians.
GEO-MEDIAN-01.try: Mark the midpoint and the centroid 2:1 ratio before introducing coordinates.
GEO-MEDIAN-01.contrast: A generic cevian is not a median unless the opposite side is actually bisected.
GEO-MEDIAN-01.example: If median AM=9, then AG=6 and GM=3.

GEO-CEVIAN-01.remember: For D on BC with BD=m, DC=n, AD=d, AC=b, AB=c: b²m+c²n=(m+n)(d²+mn).
GEO-CEVIAN-01.link: Stewart is for an arbitrary cevian when the side split is known and no more special theorem applies.
GEO-CEVIAN-01.why: It is a metric balance obtained by eliminating the altitude after applying cosine/Pythagorean relations to the two sub-triangles.
GEO-CEVIAN-01.notice: A vertex-to-side segment with a known non-midpoint split.
GEO-CEVIAN-01.contrast: If the cevian is a median, angle bisector, or altitude, try the special theorem first.
GEO-CEVIAN-01.example: If BD=DC, Stewart reduces to Apollonius.

GEO-ABIS-01.link: Arc midpoints and equal-angle constructions can create an angle bisector indirectly.
GEO-ABIS-01.why: Triangles ABD and ACD share the same altitude to BC; their area ratio equals BD/DC. Using 1/2 ab sin C and equal split angles also gives AB/AC.
GEO-ABIS-01.notice: Equal angles at a vertex, arc midpoint symmetry, or a side-ratio target.
GEO-ABIS-01.try: Confirm AD really bisects the full angle, then write the side ratio.
GEO-ABIS-01.contrast: Do not use the theorem for an exterior angle or approximate visual bisector without proof.
GEO-ABIS-01.example: If AB:AC=3:5, then an internal angle bisector divides BC in ratio 3:5.

GEO-CENTER-01.remember: Incenter = angle bisectors, equidistant from sides; circumcenter = perpendicular bisectors, equidistant from vertices; orthocenter = altitudes. ∠BHC=180°-A, ∠BIC=90°+A/2.
GEO-CENTER-01.link: “Midpoint + perpendicular” should trigger circumcenter; “equal distances to sides” should trigger incenter.
GEO-CENTER-01.why: Each center is defined by a locus intersection, so one construction fact often identifies the center immediately.
GEO-CENTER-01.notice: Perpendicular bisectors, altitudes, angle bisectors, or named H/I/O.
GEO-CENTER-01.try: Write the defining lines of the named center before using any derived angle formula.
GEO-CENTER-01.contrast: A point drawn near the middle is not automatically a center.
GEO-CENTER-01.example: A point on the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC satisfies OA=OB=OC.

GEO-CEVA-01.remember: For D∈BC, E∈CA, F∈AB, AD,BE,CF are concurrent iff (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB)=1.
GEO-CEVA-01.link: The product comes from area ratios; those same ratios can encode area weights around the concurrency point.
GEO-CEVA-01.why: Each side ratio can be expressed as a ratio of two small triangle areas sharing an altitude. Multiplying cancels all intermediate areas.
GEO-CEVA-01.notice: Three cevians + side-division ratios + concurrency target.
GEO-CEVA-01.try: Write the three side ratios in cyclic order and check whether two already determine the third.
GEO-CEVA-01.contrast: Use Menelaus, not Ceva, when the target is collinearity of three side-line points.
GEO-CEVA-01.example: If BD/DC=2/3 and CE/EA=3/4, concurrency forces AF/FB=2.

GEO-MENELAUS-01.remember: For a line through D∈BC, E∈CA, F on AB or its extension, directed ratios satisfy (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB)=-1.
GEO-MENELAUS-01.link: The formula resembles Ceva, but the geometry is different: one line across the three side-lines.
GEO-MENELAUS-01.why: Directed segment ratios preserve the sign change caused by an external division point.
GEO-MENELAUS-01.notice: Three collinear points on the side-lines of one triangle.
GEO-MENELAUS-01.try: Draw the point order and choose one signed-segment convention before calculating.
GEO-MENELAUS-01.contrast: Do not drop the sign until the end if an extension point is involved.
GEO-MENELAUS-01.example: If two positive internal ratios multiply to 6, the directed third ratio must be -1/6.

GEO-CIRCLE-01.remember: Central angle = 2×inscribed angle on the same arc. Diameter subtends 90°. Cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles sum to 180°. Equal chords subtend equal angles.
GEO-CIRCLE-01.link: Always name the chord/arc being subtended; that prevents many wrong-angle transfers.
GEO-CIRCLE-01.why: Inscribed angles measuring the same arc are locked to the same half-central angle.
GEO-CIRCLE-01.notice: Four concyclic points, diameter, equal chords/arcs, or repeated angles subtending the same segment.
GEO-CIRCLE-01.try: Circle the relevant chord and mark which two angles see it.
GEO-CIRCLE-01.contrast: Prove cyclicity before using cyclic properties.
GEO-CIRCLE-01.example: If ∠ACB=37° in a circle, then the central angle ∠AOB on the same minor arc is 74°.

GEO-POWER-01.remember: Interior chords: PA·PB=PC·PD. Tangent-secant: PT²=PA·PB, where PB is the whole secant distance.
GEO-POWER-01.link: Power is a product invariant. The picture decides which product form is legal.
GEO-POWER-01.why: Similar triangles formed by the intersecting chords/secant geometry produce the product equality.
GEO-POWER-01.notice: Two chords through one point, two secants from one external point, or a tangent plus secant.
GEO-POWER-01.try: Label near and far secant endpoints so “whole secant” cannot be confused with the inside piece.
GEO-POWER-01.contrast: The most common error is using only the inside part of a secant.
GEO-POWER-01.example: If PT=6 and PA=4, then PB=9 because 36=4·PB.

GEO-PTOLEMY-01.remember: For cyclic ABCD in order: AC·BD=AB·CD+BC·AD.
GEO-PTOLEMY-01.link: It is especially strong in a square or regular pentagon because several side/diagonal lengths repeat.
GEO-PTOLEMY-01.why: Ptolemy converts a cyclic quadrilateral into one exact length equation without introducing angles.
GEO-PTOLEMY-01.notice: Cyclic quadrilateral + many known/equal chord lengths + a diagonal/side expression.
GEO-PTOLEMY-01.try: Write the vertices in cyclic order and identify both diagonals before substituting.
GEO-PTOLEMY-01.contrast: Do not use Ptolemy on an arbitrary quadrilateral.
GEO-PTOLEMY-01.example: For a rectangle with sides 5 and 12, Ptolemy gives d²=25+144, so d=13.
